newsitem.title: USA: Albright, Qian to meet on summit.
newsitem.headline: Albright, Qian to meet on summit.

text.p: Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, enroute to Asia on Thursday, was to meet Chinese Qian Qichen for new talks aimed at preparing for an increasingly important Sino-U.S. summit in Washington that officials say has been tentatively agreed for Oct. 28.
Although officials have previously said the summit between U.S. President Bill Clinton and Chinese President Jiang Zemin would be in October, a specific date has not been formally announced.
Officials say privately Oct. 28 is being discussed.

Albright, who is due to arrive in Kuala Lumpur on Friday, is to meet on Saturday with Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen on the fringes of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) annual meeting.
ASEAN is expected to focus heavily on the crisis caused in Cambodia when strongman Hun Sen staged a coup on July 6, and that is also expected to come up in the Qian-Albright meeting.
Speaking to reporters on Albright's aircraft, State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns welcomed Hun Sen's decision to reverse his earlier position and permit mediation of the conflict by ASEAN.

But he challenged Hun Sen to translate deeds into actions and said while Hun Sen "controls Cambodia", Washington would continue to oppose his efforts to seize power unilaterally by insisting Hun Sen re-establish a coalition government, restore democracy and let opponents participate in politics.

Burns was noncommital about whether the United States would accept Hun Sen's appointment of Foreign Minister Ung Huot as prime minister, replacing Prince Norodom Ranarridh, if approved by parliament. Burns said Washington wanted to be sure the process met constitutional norms and was free of intimidation.
A delegation of U.S. officials who are experts on Asia was in Beijing this week for working level talks on the summit and some will join Albright in Malaysia to brief her on their meetings.
One official called the Clinton-Jiang summit the "most important meeting between the two countries in a decade."
China, the world's most populous country, is on track to be one of the largest economies and a world power.

Despite a continuing scandal in Washington on allegations of Chinese efforts to influence the 1996 U.S. election, U.S. officials are upbeat about the current process of engagement with Beijing that is intended to keep ties improving after a period of dangerously deteriorating relations.
A series of events is set up "that guarantees the best possible behaviour by China" and is aimed at keeping the relationship moving forward, an official said.
One major watershed was the Chinese takeover of Hong Kong from British rule on July 1, which Washington considers a litmus test for Sino-American ties.
U.S. officials give Beijing high marks for how the actual handover was conducted, but are continuing to watch how the economic powerhouse's life under communism evolves.
The Washington summit is another milestone, and a return summit in Beijing expected for the first half of 1998 is a third.

U.S. officials say Beijing may be more interested in the process and pomp of a summit, at which Jiang is received at the White House in a formal ceremony, but they are pushing for concrete achievements in key areas, including human rights and nonproliferation.
Albright recently has made a point of praising progress with Beijing on nonproliferation issues and lauding cooperation on such matters as bringing North Korea into peace talks.
On Saturday, Albright is also due to hold a trilateral meeting with the foreign ministers of Indonesia, Thailand and the Philippines who have been trying to mediate for ASEAN on Cambodia.
